results.response_text:
Evan Huang is a software engineer currently working at Capital One, where he has been a Software Engineer since August 2023. Prior to this, he also completed Software Engineering Internships at Capital One in the summers of 2021 and 2022.

His work at Capital One includes building "Recadero," a Go CLI that significantly reduces boilerplate and prevents schema drift in production services, and developing a billing-cycle management action for credit card processing. He also designed an event-driven card transaction processing system with Go, Restate, Lambda, and Kafka, focusing on quick recovery times and idempotent processing. Furthermore, he contributed to preapproval and eligibility flows for a small-business credit card platform, leading to substantial annualized value and conversion lift. He also created "crumb," a Go CLI and Claude Code skill that links requirements with implementation and tests, and developed automated code-review and Jira-workflow tools that saved significant engineering hours.

During his internships, Evan Huang built a Scala/ZIO verification layer for an internal card transaction ledger, validating billions of records, and developed a Spark/Scala pipeline to identify untracked DynamoDB datasets.

Beyond Capital One, Evan Huang was the founder of HashTop from 2020 to 2023, a cryptocurrency mining platform that generated considerable revenue. He also describes himself as a "solo dev shipping products end to end," with projects spanning embedded firmware, web applications, and local AI, including building cave-survey devices and backend services. His personal projects include "HostelHound" for hostel price history and predictions, "Camazotz" for designing and selling cave diving equipment, "FinFeed" for live fish-tank camera streaming, and "geo-daemon" for tracking brand visibility across AI search engines. He also developed "Pi Notes," a TypeScript extension for preserving coding-agent task states.

Evan Huang is pursuing an MS in Computer Science at New York University (2023–2025) and previously earned a BA in Computer Science & Economics from New York University (2019–2023). He specializes in languages and technologies such as Go, Python, Kafka, Restate, AWS, React, Scala, ZIO, Spark, DynamoDB, PostgreSQL, C++, HTML5, and CSS3. His GitHub profile highlights his work in distributed systems, developer tooling, and underwater hardware.

results.response_text:
Evan Huang is involved in significant projects focused on autonomous underwater cave exploration and mapping, primarily through his contributions to the RoboPI lab's initiatives, including CaveSeg and CL-ViT. These projects aim to overcome the challenges of mapping dangerous and inaccessible underwater cave environments using advanced robotics and artificial intelligence.

His work contributes to the development of cutting-edge visual learning pipelines and robotic systems for:
*   **Semantic Segmentation and Scene Parsing (CaveSeg)**: This project focuses on enabling Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) to understand and interpret underwater cave environments in real-time. It involves creating comprehensive datasets with pixel annotations for crucial navigation elements like cavelines, arrows, and open areas for visual servoing, as well as identifying obstacles such as the ground plane and overhead layers. The goal is to develop computationally light, transformer-based models that allow AUVs to navigate autonomously and avoid collisions.
*   **Caveline Detection and Following (CL-ViT Project)**: This initiative is vital for robot navigation guidance during autonomous cave mapping missions. It involves a novel Vision Transformer (ViT)-based learning pipeline designed for fast and accurate detection of cavelines in images from underwater caves. A weakly supervised approach facilitates rapid model adaptation to data from new locations with minimal ground truth labels, and its effectiveness has been validated in cave systems across the USA, Mexico, and Spain.
*   **3D Topography Mapping and Data Collection**: The autonomous robots developed through these projects assist human divers by collecting water quality data and comprehensive topography mapping information. This capability allows for the exploration of previously uncharted territories and the revelation of archaeological mysteries within these critical groundwater systems.

Evan Huang's work, in collaboration with researchers like Dr. Ioannis Rekleitis and Dr. Ramtin Zand, focuses on enhancing the autonomy and safety of underwater cave exploration. By enabling robots to navigate and map these complex environments independently, the projects aim to reduce the risks to human divers and contribute to a better understanding of karst topographies, which are vital freshwater resources globally.

results.response_text:
Evan Huang's underwater cave mapping project is Camazotz (specifically the Cave Mapper system) , a custom-built handheld device and gear line designed to provide real-time navigation and 3D mapping during overhead cave dives.
Key Features of the Cave Mapper System
Real-Time Navigation: Offers live spatial tracking and navigation guidance while swimming through underwater cave passages.
Sensor Suite: Combines a magnetic encoder for distance tracking, a 9-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU) for orientation, and a precision depth sensor.
Firmware & Hardware: Built using Fusion for modeling, an RP2350 microcontroller running C firmware, and custom-designed housings (including ASA 3D-printed reels, spools, and line markers) . Spinlocks protect cross-core state, and navigation calculations run directly from SRAM to avoid flash-cache latency.
Data Export & Visualization: Exports survey data into standard cave-mapping formats such as Compass and Walls, with web visualization support at Camazotz Map .

DIY and open-source underwater cave mapping hardware and mobile-assisted toolkits are developed by several project creators combining 3D-printed mechanics with smartphone or micro-controller sensors:
CaveDiveMap (f0xdude): An open-source project combining an iOS smartphone (housed in an affordable waterproof dive case like the DiveVolk Seatouch 4) with a custom 3D-printed mechanical wheel device. The wheel clamps directly onto the cave guideline; as the diver swims, rotations convert to distance while internal smartphone sensors log headings, depths, and Left/Right/Up/Down (LRUD) passage dimensions . It exports to CSV, Therion centerlines, and PLY point clouds.
The Cave Pearl Project: An ongoing open-source DIY platform built around low-cost microcontrollers (such as Arduino-based components) and custom waterproof housings test-rated for sub-aquatic environments down to 30 meters. While primarily focused on long-term environmental and flow monitoring, it acts as a modular foundation for custom underwater data loggers.
Dry/Land-to-Water Open-Source Survey Hybrids (e.g., Shetland Attack Pony / Caveatron ecosystem creators): Innovators in the open-source dry caving community (such as Phil Underwood's work on the Shetland Attack Pony and the LiDAR/survey units) have influenced portable, low-cost sensor design, with builders like Addison Snyder adapting open-source SLAM and LiDAR concepts toward experimental underwater enclosure prototypes.

The Camazotz Cave Mapping Project refers to the development of the Cave Mapper System, a specialized hardware and software project created by the technical dive group Camazotz Diving .
The project's goal is to provide certified underwater cave explorers with a way to generate detailed, real-time 3D maps of underwater caves while swimming.
How the Mapping System Works
The system acts as a compact data-logging device attached to a diver's equipment. As the diver swims through a flooded cave system, a dual-core processor combines multiple sensor inputs 100 times per second to track movement and geometry:
Depth Profiling: Uses a high-precision pressure transducer to track vertical movement.
Distance Tracking: Uses a magnetic encoder connected to a survey line wheel to measure how far the diver has traveled.
Heading and Orientation: Utilizes a 9-axis Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) and compass to record direction and pitch.
Data Processing and Visualization
During the dive, the system plots a real-time "stick map" of the diver’s path. After returning to the surface, the logged data can be uploaded directly to the browser-based Camazotz Cave Mapping Software . The software then processes the data to export:
2D passage profiles (both top-down "plan" views and side cross-sections).
3D point cloud visualizations of the cave system.
Standard cave survey formats compatible with traditional mapping software like Compass and Walls.
